ai-at-work.title: AI cyber resilience and the trust gap
ai-at-work.excerpt: Backup and recovery has evolved into data protection, security and cyber recovery. Today, the focus is on business resilience. The scope continues to expand, with growing attention to how attackers us
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A new study highlights how AI is reshaping both cyber attacks and defenses, with the conversation shifting from just backing up data to building overall business resilience against AI-powered threats. Digital workplace leaders need to understand this evolution because their networks, content, and employee access are now targets for increasingly sophisticated AI-driven attacks. Here's the honest take: most organizations are still patching yesterday's problems while hackers are already three steps ahead with machine learning, which means your cyber strategy needs to evolve faster than your last Slack update.

ai-at-work.title: The AI boom’s missing balance-sheet question: What has actually been verified?
ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence infrastructure commitments are growing faster than the evidence connecting contracted capacity to sustained economic value. I spent 13 years on the floor of the New York Stock
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Companies are committing massive budgets to AI infrastructure without solid proof that it's actually delivering measurable business returns. This matters to us in digital workplace because we're often the ones asked to justify these expensive AI implementations to skeptical executives who've already blown money on failed tech initiatives. The honest truth is we're living in a "trust me bro" moment with AI spending, and eventually someone's CFO is going to demand receipts we don't have.

ai-at-work.title: Atomicwork launches certified AI coworker marketplace for enterprise IT and security
ai-at-work.excerpt: Information technology service management startup Atomicwork Inc. today announced the launch of an Artificial Intelligence Coworker Marketplace that will give enterprise IT and security teams access t
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Atomicwork launched a marketplace of prebuilt AI agents designed to handle specific IT and security tasks like cloud management and access control. This matters because IT teams are drowning in repetitive work, and certified, ready-to-deploy AI could actually free people up to do something that requires a human brain. The real test is whether these "coworkers" stay certified once they hit the messy reality of your actual enterprise environment.

ai-at-work.title: Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M, releases new AI productivity features
ai-at-work.excerpt: Dropbox Inc. is acquiring cloud storage startup Tigris Data Inc. for $350 million. The company announced the deal today in conjunction with a major update to its product portfolio. It introduced DBX A
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Dropbox just dropped 350 million dollars to buy Tigris Data and rolled out new AI features including something called DBX Agent Cloud, which basically lets AI agents store their own data. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because it signals that every major productivity platform is now racing to embed AI agents directly into their infrastructure rather than bolting them on afterward. Look, I've seen a lot of acquisitions over three decades, and when you're paying this much for a relatively unknown startup, you're not buying their product, you're buying their talent and their vision for where this is all headed.

tools-tech.title: Google Pics: How to level up your visuals in Docs and Slides
tools-tech.excerpt: Simplicity and convenience are a tough combo to beat. That’s why basic features integrated into the productivity apps we’re already using almost always win out over more capable and complex third-part
tools-tech.dwp_take: Google added a simpler image search and insertion tool directly into Docs and Slides so users don't have to leave the app or hunt through third-party plugins. This matters because digital workplace professionals are always fighting against tool sprawl and context switching, so anything that keeps people in their primary workflow reduces friction and improves actual productivity output. Honestly, this is the kind of boring, incremental improvement that actually changes behavior more than any flashy AI feature ever will, which probably explains why it's already being ignored by half your organization.

digital-culture.title: The memo was never the point. The point was to clarify your thinking
digital-culture.excerpt: In 2004, Jeff Bezos banned PowerPoint from Amazon’s senior leadership meetings in favor of narrative memos, read in silence at the start of each meeting. The idea was that a well-structured and tightl
digital-culture.dwp_take: Jeff Bezos banned PowerPoint at Amazon in 2004, replacing it with narrative memos that leaders read silently before meetings to force clearer thinking. This matters because digital workplace tools often become the point instead of serving the actual work, and most organizations still assume flashy slides equal better communication when they usually just hide fuzzy thinking. Here's the thing: Amazon's memo culture worked because it demanded rigor, not because memos are inherently superior. Most teams would rather grab a template and call it done.

digital-culture.title: As employer burnout costs soar, EY gets at the heart of worker well-being with Vitality Index
digital-culture.excerpt: The tool is designed to help employers measure and boost workforce well-being.
digital-culture.dwp_take: EY launched a Vitality Index tool to help employers measure and track workforce well-being metrics. This matters because digital workplace leaders are finally getting concrete data instead of guessing whether their remote work policies and collaboration tools are actually helping people or just creating more Slack notifications to ignore. The irony is that most companies will probably implement this tool perfectly while continuing to schedule meetings during lunch and expecting Slack responses within five minutes.

industry-news.excerpt: Cursor's new Build Live Apps feature creates and deploys web applications with databases, authentication, and hosting. Here's what's included and what it costs. The post Cursor Can Now Build and Deplo
industry-news.dwp_take: Cursor just rolled out Build Live Apps, a feature that lets you prompt your way to a fully deployed web application complete with databases, authentication, and hosting baked in. This matters because your developers and citizen developers are about to get very uncomfortable conversations with their managers about why they need those six-month timelines when the tool just shipped an app in six minutes. Look, I've seen a lot of "this changes everything" tools come and go, but when your intern can deploy production apps faster than you can schedule a standup, something has genuinely shifted.

industry-news.title: Perplexity Teammates Launches: How Its $200-a-Month AI Agents Work
industry-news.excerpt: Perplexity's new Teammates AI agents can manage ongoing tasks and work through connected apps. Here's how they work, what they cost, and who gets access. The post Perplexity Teammates Launches: How It
industry-news.dwp_take: Perplexity just launched Teammates, AI agents that handle recurring tasks across connected applications for $200 a month. This matters to digital workplace pros because autonomous agents are becoming real tools now, not lab experiments, which means we need to figure out governance, security, and integration strategies before they're everywhere. Honestly, if your org is paying $200 a month to have AI do work, you better make sure it's not just creating more problems for your IT and compliance teams to untangle.

industry-news.title: EU looks to bolster domestic chip production with €525m EuroCDP investment
industry-news.excerpt: The European Chip Design Platform (EuroCDP) aims to bolster manufacturing capabilities in the face of competition from the US and China
industry-news.dwp_take: The EU is throwing 525 million euros at the European Chip Design Platform to shore up its own semiconductor manufacturing and reduce dependence on US and Chinese suppliers. This matters to digital workplace leaders because chip shortages have been real productivity killers for years, and having regional supply chains means fewer delays when you're trying to deploy new hardware or infrastructure. Look, I've watched enough supply chain disasters to know that betting on homegrown chip capacity is smart play, though I'd argue the EU probably should have done this about ten years ago when everyone else saw this coming.

industry-news.title: Dropbox targets AI infrastructure gains with $350m Tigris Data acquisition
industry-news.excerpt: The acquisition will underpin the launch of Dropbox’s new DBX Agent Cloud service
industry-news.dwp_take: Dropbox just dropped $350 million to buy Tigris Data, a data infrastructure startup, so they can build out their new DBX Agent Cloud service. This matters because it signals that content platforms are getting serious about AI infrastructure, which means your digital workplace tool stack is about to get a lot more complicated with agents doing work across your systems. Here's the thing though: most organizations still can't manage their basic file governance, so watching them layer autonomous AI agents on top of messy data repositories should be entertaining in that tragic Greek drama kind of way.
